greeting: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who walks in our midst even when we feel alone.
penitential:

Lord, you invite us to return to our first love: Lord, have mercy.

homily:
Imagine, for a moment, the sound of a crowd. It is a chaotic, shifting, overwhelming noise. In today’s Gospel, Jesus is approaching Jericho, and the air is thick with the press of people. It is the sound of a thousand voices, the shuffle of sandals on dust, the murmur of speculation. And there, sitting by the roadside, is a man who cannot see. He is a man who knows this sound intimately—the sound of a world that is moving on without him. He is a beggar, someone the world has relegated to the margins, someone whose life is defined by what he lacks. But then, he hears the most important thing he has ever heard. He hears that Jesus of Nazareth is passing by.

He does not ask for money. He does not ask for bread. He shouts, 'Jesus, Son of David, have pity on me!' The crowd—that same crowd that was just a moment ago a wall of noise—tries to push him back. They tell him to be quiet. They tell him to stay in his place. But he calls out all the more. He is desperate, yes, but he is also profoundly, courageously awake. He knows that his one chance to be truly seen is standing just a few feet away. And Jesus, who hears the single, lonely voice over the roar of the multitude, stops. He stops everything. He orders the man to be brought to him. And then, he asks the most gentle, the most human of questions: 'What do you want me to do for you?'

I want you to hold onto this image: the man by the roadside. It is the image of a soul who is waiting for the Lord to stop and notice him. It is the image of Benjamin Vo. Think of Benjamin’s life—a life of such extraordinary, quiet brilliance. Think of the way his mind worked, not just in the cold logic of mathematics or the complex architecture of cloud infrastructure, but in the way he understood the world. He was a boy who loved the mechanics of things, the way a Boeing 737 lifts off the runway, the way a line of code creates a game, the way a family moves together through the cities of the world. He was a boy who was always looking, always observing, always learning. He was a boy who saw beauty in the details that others missed. He was a boy who, even at fifteen, understood that the most important things in life aren't the things we can touch, but the things we can offer.

Let us tell the truth of the heart before we look for the comfort. Alan, Thao, Ryan, and all of you who hold the memory of Benjamin as a sacred trust: it has been five months since he went home to God. We know the reality of your quiet house. We know the moments when the silence becomes a weight, when the habits of a lifetime—the quick laugh, the bright smile with the braces, the way he would share his thoughts about his 'con chim airlines'—are suddenly met with an empty space. You are grieving. You are carrying a cross that is heavy, real, and unrelenting. You are allowed to be tired. You are allowed to feel the sudden ache when a memory ambushes you in the middle of an ordinary Tuesday. Do not pretend the weight is lighter than it is. Do not rush to be ‘strong’ for the sake of others if your heart is currently breaking. Your honesty before God is the most authentic prayer you can offer. Your tears are not a lack of faith; they are the language of love that has no place left to go.

And let us gently lift one particular stone from your hearts today—a stone that grief often slips into our pockets without us noticing. Sometimes, when a family suffers an unimaginable loss, the mind begins to circle back, whispering quiet, unfair questions. Did we miss a sign? Could we have done something more? Could we have watched closer? Let us lay that burden down right here at the altar. You missed nothing. You loved Benjamin with a completeness that filled his fifteen years with the richness of a lifetime—traveling the globe together from the streets of Beijing to the sacred grottoes of Lourdes, sharing quiet stories, and walking side by side as a family of four. You were the exact parents and the exact brother that Benjamin needed. Let that heavy stone fall; you are absolved, and you are held. You did not fail him in any way. You were the light in his life, just as he was the light in yours. Some things in this life are simply beyond our control, and God does not hold you responsible for the mysteries of the cross. You are held in His mercy, not judged by your sorrow. You are not to blame for the randomness of the world’s suffering. You are simply loved.

Now, let the Gospel break into that quiet room. Jesus stops for the blind man, and he stops for you. He asks, 'What do you want me to do for you?' It is a question that invites us to be honest. It is a question that invites us to stop pretending. Maybe today, your answer is simple. Maybe your answer is just, 'Lord, help me to get through this afternoon.' Maybe your answer is, 'Lord, help me to see my brother Ryan, to love him, to be there for him.' Maybe your answer is, 'Lord, let me feel Benjamin’s presence again.' Jesus does not turn away from that longing. He honors it. He takes the blind man’s request—'Lord, please let me see'—and he gives him back the world. He gives him back the ability to walk, to follow, to give glory to God. Benjamin is now seeing with a clarity that we cannot yet imagine. He is seeing the face of the Lord, the one he loved and served with his gentle, curious heart. He is not lost in the dark; he is standing in the light. He is watching over you, and he is cheering for you to keep walking, to keep hoping, to keep being the family that he loved so dearly.

Consider the first reading from Revelation: 'I know your works, your labor, and your endurance... you have endurance and have suffered for my name, and you have not grown weary.' This is a word for you. You have been through so much. You have endured the unthinkable, and yet, you are still here, still gathering, still loving, still remembering. You have not grown weary in your love for Benjamin. You keep his memory alive in such beautiful, quiet ways. Think of the 'Well of Love' in Cà Mau, that clean water flowing in his name, bringing life to those who were thirsty. That is the work of a life that continues to bear fruit. That is the way Benjamin’s kindness ripples out into the world, touching the lives of people he never met, in a place he may never have walked. His life was not a brief flicker; it was a fire that continues to burn.

Ryan, you are a brother who carries a unique, holy weight. You know the memories better than anyone. You know the shared laughter, the way you both looked out the window on those train rides, the way you navigated the world together. You are not just a brother who remains; you are a brother who continues the story. When you look at the sky, when you think of the future, remember that you are not doing it alone. You are carrying the legacy of his joy. You are a witness to the world that love is not a finite resource. It is a well that never runs dry. Keep being the boy who reaches out. Keep being the one who values the small, human moments. You are a vital part of this family of four, and your life is a testament to the fact that love is the most durable thing we possess. Your brother's love is not gone; it is woven into the very fabric of who you are becoming. He is cheering for you, and he is walking with you in the quiet places of your heart.

We hear in the Psalm today: 'He is like a tree planted near running water, that yields its fruit in due season, and whose leaves never fade.' This is the turn of the heart. The blessing of the Lord is not that we will never suffer, but that we will never be abandoned in our suffering. Benjamin is now resting in that promise. He is dwelling in the land of the living, fully alive, fully healed, and fully embraced by the Father. He is not a memory tucked away in a photo album; he is a living soul in the Banquet of Heaven, standing alongside kindred spirits, watching over you with a love that has been purified and perfected. Think of the dream Alan had, where Ben and his dad stood outside room 419, and Ben said with that earnest voice, 'Ba ơi, test nào con cũng qua hết... Không sao đâu, con sẽ dõi theo ba mẹ.' That dream was a whisper from heaven. It was the assurance that he has passed every test, that he is whole, and that he is watching over you with a smile. He is the one who has already crossed the threshold into the light, and he is cheering you on.

There is a peace that comes from knowing that we are held. It is not a peace that takes away the pain overnight, but it is a peace that keeps us from being destroyed by it. It is the peace of knowing that Benjamin is waiting. He is waiting in the light, waiting in the place where there is no more struggling, only the clear, bright presence of God. He is waiting for you with that same sweet, gentle smile that you remember so vividly. That smile is the promise that the reunion is certain. He is a light in the world, and he is shining for you. He is home. And because he is home, you are never truly lost. He is holding the key to that reunion, and he is waiting for the day when the family of four is whole again in the house of the Father.

To everyone tuning in from afar—especially other children who are carrying heavy crosses of suffering, and every family whose home feels too quiet today—hear this: you are seen by God. You are not forgotten. The Lord draws closest to the brokenhearted, and His mercy is broad enough to hold every single one of our tears. You are not a broken family. You are a family of four, and you are being held in the palm of God's hand.

So, what do you carry out the door today? Not a summary, not a heavy burden, but one small, doable thing: when the grief rises and the house feels too quiet, pause. Close your eyes. Breathe in. Imagine the Lord reaching into the silence, and imagine Benjamin standing beside you, smiling that bright, easy grin, looking out toward an endless horizon, dreaming of his next journey. Let yourself be gathered into the peace of Christ. Walk out knowing that you are loved, that you are not to blame, and that the one who went before you is waiting at the door of eternity. Keep your heart open to that truth. Keep your eyes on the light. And remember that he is watching over you, always, with love that knows no end. Amen.
spiritual_communion: My Jesus, I believe that you are present in the Most Holy Sacrament. I love you above all things, and I desire to receive you into my soul. Since I cannot at this moment receive you sacramentally, come at least spiritually into my heart. I embrace you as if you were already there and unite myself wholly to you. Never permit me to be separated from you. Amen.
closing: May the Lord bless you and keep you, may He let His face shine upon you and be gracious to you, and may He give you His peace. In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.
standing_petitions: For our beloved Benjamin Vo, and for all who have gone before us marked with the sign of faith, that they may rest forever in the light of Christ’s presence.
For all who are grieving and carrying the heavy cross of loss, that God may console their hearts, strengthen their spirits, and fill them with the hope of the Resurrection.

readings.label: Reading 1
readings.text:
The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave to him,
to show his servants what must happen soon.
He made it known by sending his angel to his servant John,
who gives witness to the word of God
and to the testimony of Jesus Christ by reporting what he saw.
Blessed is the one who reads aloud
and blessed are those who listen to this prophetic message
and heed what is written in it, for the appointed time is near.John, to the seven churches in Asia: grace to you and peace
from him who is and who was and who is to come,
and from the seven spirits before his throne.I heard the Lord saying to me:
“To the angel of the Church in Ephesus, write this:“‘The one who holds the seven stars in his right hand
and walks in the midst of the seven gold lampstands says this:
“I know your works, your labor, and your endurance,
and that you cannot tolerate the wicked;
you have tested those who call themselves Apostles but are not,
and discovered that they are impostors.
Moreover, you have endurance and have suffered for my name,
and you have not grown weary.
Yet I hold this against you:
you have lost the love you had at first.
Realize how far you have fallen.
Repent, and do the works you did at first.
Otherwise, I will come to you
and remove your lampstand from its place, unless you repent.”’”

readings.label: Responsorial Psalm
readings.text:
R. (Rev. 2:17) Those who are victorious I will feed from the tree of life.
Blessed the man who follows not
the counsel of the wicked
Nor walks in the way of sinners,
nor sits in the company of the insolent,
But delights in the law of the LORD
and meditates on his law day and night.
R. Those who are victorious I will feed from the tree of life.
He is like a tree
planted near running water,
That yields its fruit in due season,
and whose leaves never fade.
Whatever he does, prospers.
R. Those who are victorious I will feed from the tree of life.
Not so the wicked, not so;
they are like chaff which the wind drives away.
For the LORD watches over the way of the just,
but the way of the wicked vanishes.
R. Those who are victorious I will feed from the tree of life.

readings.label: Gospel
readings.text:
As Jesus approached Jericho
a blind man was sitting by the roadside begging,
and hearing a crowd going by, he inquired what was happening.
They told him,
“Jesus of Nazareth is passing by.”
He shouted, “Jesus, Son of David, have pity on me!”
The people walking in front rebuked him,
telling him to be silent,
but he kept calling out all the more,
“Son of David, have pity on me!”
Then Jesus stopped and ordered that he be brought to him;
and when he came near, Jesus asked him,
“What do you want me to do for you?”
He replied, “Lord, please let me see.”
Jesus told him, “Have sight; your faith has saved you.”
He immediately received his sight
and followed him, giving glory to God.
When they saw this, all the people gave praise to God.
